item.title: Who’s Tom Petty?
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: Yes, someone actually asked me that. We were talking about concerts we’d been to and I referenced him at the once-of Pemberton Festival in Canada, and just got a blank stare. I’m not sure if it’s worse or better that I followed up, eyebrow raised with “y’know…Last Dance With Mary Jane…Free Fallin’?” and got “oh [...]
item.content:encoded:
Yes, someone actually asked me that.  We were talking about concerts we’d been to and I referenced him at the once-of Pemberton Festival in Canada, and just got a blank stare.  I’m not sure if it’s worse or better that I followed up, eyebrow raised with “y’know…Last Dance With Mary Jane…Free Fallin’?” and got “oh yeah, sure I know those” without pressing to verify they weren’t just saying that to get the horrified look off my face.

Fine, I'll just go listen to Tom Petty by myself!

I believe it was Plato who famously complained about the youths these days, and having been proven wrong over thousands of years it’s something I make a conscious effort to try not to say or believe even if deep down I sympathize.  Being in the college town of Gainesville, home to the University of Florida (yes, Tim Tebow’s alma matter, we’ll skip that commentary here) I figured it only made sense to CouchSurf with some college kids, so I broke my rule of not seeking out people more than 5 years my junior.  Oh I don’t regret it, we went to an Oregon Trail themed party and a rager house party with 50 people at a three bedroom house mainly spilling out onto the street.  There was even a dude with a mullet and a shirt that read GAINESVILLE FUCKING FLORIDA!

However, because this is the American south, the term we use in Canada called “student ghetto” still applies, but in a literal sense.  A transient kid population just looking for a cheap place to live begets slum lords, rundown properties and depressed values, which in turn causes actual riff raff to move in.  I didn’t really think much of some of the neighbours coming over and crashing the party, other than laughing that kids had the audacity to complain when there was blaring music and 40 people blocking the street at two in the morning.  Soon enough someone had ordered a Jimmy John sandwich, the delivery boy propped his bike on the side of the house when he went in to deliver it, then found it gone when he came back outside.  Quickly borrowing someone else’s bike to search for his own, after some minutes he angrily sped back towards the full crowd, someone stepped in his way and he totally wiped in front of all the cool kids and threw his helmet against the wall screaming he would shit in their sandwich if they ever ordered one to that house again.

***

“What’s espresso?”

For some reason this question from the person in front of me in line brought a beaming grin to my face, unlike the Tom Petty inquiry.  It was in response to the scripted sales pitch at McDonald’s for their new McCafe deal, and if it wasn’t for the piece of paper to answer, I’m pretty sure the cashier didn’t know either.  By this point in time I was in the absolute middle of nowhere in the Florida panhandle, returning from another adventure of camping in the middle of nowhere (best spot ever FYI, check the gallery).  It was the only McDonald’s for 50 miles in any direction, there probably wasn’t a Starbucks, or for that matter an espresso maker for at least 100, and I’m not sure why, but I like that, even though I like espresso, and Starbucks.

The Gulf

What I didn’t like was hearing the 6 year old kid in the booth next to me make reference to “the 51 states” and not be corrected by her mother.  I mean, maybe Puerto Rico counts because this is Florida, but these were white country folks in the panhandle.  Somehow miraculously diffusing the reaction growing in my mind was the fact I was drawn into it as the mother turned to me and asked while pointing to the parking lot “what state does that license plate say, New York?”  It was very far away, but I have fighter pilot vision and have been able to beat anyone reading the letters at a distance since I was a child, so after a brief squint I informed her “no ma’am, Michigan”.  Thank God Bessie was out of view so we didn’t have to get into which state Alberta was.

item.title: MPPT Charge Controller
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: This is the sixth DIY solar post in a series on solar power systems detailing the role of the solar charge controller and why to prefer an MPPT charge controller. While this application was done for an RV solar panel system, the concepts are intended to apply for any do it yourself solar power system. [...]
item.content:encoded:
This is the sixth DIY solar post in a series on solar power systems detailing the role of the solar charge controller and why to prefer an MPPT charge controller.  While this application was done for an RV solar panel system, the concepts are intended to apply for any do it yourself solar power system.  We hope you enjoy this entry (The Solar Series: Choosing a Solar Charge Controller) and links to the rest of the DIY solar panel system series can be found at the bottom.

This post will outline why we need a charge controller in the first place by explaining what it does, then go into a comparison of which technology is best, detail some practical sizing and wiring considerations then finish with an explanation of different models of charge controllers and their customizability.  Having personally used the Morningstar Tristar 45 MPPT and found it to be the most efficient, customizable and reliable, I recommend it so much it’s got its own dedicated post.

What is a Charge Controller and Why Do I Need One?

In a perfect world it would seem straightforward that we would take the wires from our solar panels, hook them up to our batteries and be done with it.  Unfortunately it’s not that simple.  Both the panels and the batteries are “dumb” and so the charge controller needs to act as a brain to keep the charging process running smoothly and efficiently.  How “smart” the controller is depends on the technology and manufacturer, but the best models will sense incoming power from the panels, the charge level and temperature of the batteries and adjust the controller’s output accordingly.  I refer to it as “smart” because in some fashion or another it needs to be able to sense these outside variables and make decisions based on them.  The two main issues it is compensating for are varying input power from the panels and varying charge levels of the battery as explained in the following two paragraphs.

The controller is the "brain"

The voltage output of a solar panel is affected by how much sunlight is striking it and at what intensity.  In the simplest case of a 12 volt nominal panel this can vary from slightly below 12 V at the crack of dawn to above 17 V in broad daylight, especially if it’s cold outside.  If your battery is moderately charged hovering around 12.5 V, it’s going to not get charged at all in the morning, then by midday it will be boiling and destroy itself.  The primary function of even the simplest charge controller is to prevent this from happening.

The second concern is the charging profile of a battery.  If it’s at 12.5 V, depending on the battery it is perhaps most happy being charged at a constant voltage of 13.8.  All the current will flow into the electrolyte ion chemical reactions to store more power.  However, eventually the battery will be full and instead of storing more charge it will get hot, start to boil and after an extended period permanently damage itself.  Any decent modern charge controller will sense the battery voltage and realize once it’s held it at 13.8 for awhile and the battery is full, it should perhaps back it down to something like 13 V to go easy on the little guy as he can’t store any more charge.  A third bonus a good charge controller can take care of here is temperature compensation, that 13.8 V might be perfect if it’s 25 OC, but if it’s -25 OC maybe it should be backed off to 13.2 V to reduce stress.

Controlling Voltage: PWM vs. MPPT

Now that we’ve outlined why the voltage needs to be shaped to suit the needs of the battery, the next question is how?  The basic method used in any modern charge controller is something called pulse width modulation (PWM).  It might sound like a scary engineering term, but it’s a simple concept.  If the panels are outputting at 17 V and I only want to charge the battery at 13.6 V, a simple solution is to have the charge controller only on 80% of the time (17*0.8=13.6).  While this is achieved with transistors that turn on and off thousands of times per second, it’s easy to visualize looking at the graph and thinking of it at a high level.

PWM in a nutshell: on and off real fast

However, pulse width modulation alone has one massive drawback here, you aren’t harvesting energy 20% of the time because the circuit is open.  Sure, it’s better than frying your battery, but it’s incredibly wasteful and inefficient.  For this reason PWM should only be considered in smaller solar installations where the cost of better technology won’t be recouped over time (explained in the next section), although good affordable PWM controllers certainly exist.

And what is this better technology?  It’s something called maximum power point tracking (the abbreviation at the front of MPPT charge controller) and is vastly superior to PWM alone.  The basic idea is through more complex and expensive power electronics in the solar charge controller it is able to act as a variable DC power supply.  So if you have 17 Volts input from the panel at a current of 10 amps (170 Watts) and still want to output that at 13.6 V, you’ll wind up with just a tad under 12.5 amps from the MPPT controller.  How this all actually works you don’t want to know, trust me (for masochist engineers: MPPT theory) but the efficiency winds up being in the 98% range, which means 10 times less loss than PWM only.

The other major benefit of an MPPT charge controller is allowing the use of higher nominal voltage solar panels.  My 36 volt panels charging 12 volt batteries would not be possible with PWM (unless you wanted 30% efficiency), but with the variable DC power supply of MPPT I’m able to do it easily with an efficiency around 96%.  The greater this step down in voltage, the less efficient the charge controller will be and the hotter it will get, but for the versatility afforded in choosing panels, improved energy recovery in low light and less ohmic loss over a 36 volt wire run, it’s more than worth it.

Expanding on this, a good MPPT charge controller doesn’t just increase efficiency on the output side by monitoring the battery charge state (PWM controllers can do this too), it can also control the input power by modifying the solar array voltage.  If you have a 36 Volt nominal array, an MPPT solar charge controller will perform a voltage sweep and see exactly what point produces optimal power.  Left to their own devices, the panels might stabilize at 42 Volts, but the MPPT charge controller could find during its voltage sweep that harvested power is highest if the panels are held at 40.5 Volts, so it will force them to stay there.

Choosing an MPPT Charge Controller

The main factors to take into account when selecting a charge controller are whether your solar power system is large enough to warrant the cost of MPPT, choosing an appropriate amp rating based on system size, and what additional charge controller features you need/want.

Voltage setpoints, yet another way to increase efficiency

The most logical way to decide on getting an MPPT charge controller vs a PWM charge controller is payout, i.e. will the increased efficiency pay for the increased cost.  Because almost all major solar panel manufacturers guarantee panel output for 25 years, that’s plenty of time to get your money back.  Let’s go through a quick example comparing my existing MPPT system versus a hypothetical PWM system.  I’ve got 430 Watts of power at 36 volts, my wire run adds a 1% loss and my Tristar MPPT charge controller is 96% efficient stepping down from 36 to 12 volts, which yields an available actual power of 409 Watts.  An equivalent 12 volt system with a PWM charge controller would have an 8% loss in the wires (thicker wire would cost more) and just to make it more fair, let’s say 85% efficient at stepping down from the array’s 15-17 volts, yielding an available actual power of 336 Watts, a 73 Watt difference.

The short way of comparing the two is taking the 73 Watts multiplied by the average solar panel value of $4 per Watt, which gives you around $300 extra dollars to spend on the charge controller.  However, a far better method of comparison is to analyze how much energy you’re losing via inefficiency over the entire lifetime of the system and what it’s worth monetarily, which tilts the scales far more in the MPPT’s favour.  If we make the assumption of 5 hours of peak sunlight a day, the math breaks down like this: 73 Watts of loss * 5 hours peak sunlight per day * 365 days * 25 years = 3.3 megawatt hours.  Yes, megawatts.  Using the solar power system as a straight up grid tie-in replacement that values the power at about $0.10 per kilowatt hour, that equates to $333, similar to our shorthand estimate.  However, in the case of my RV which is never connected to the grid, I value a kilowatt hour at a lot more than 10 cents because I can get it wherever I want, anywhere on the planet.  The same goes for an off-grid remote installation where there are no power lines.  Lastly, and even more importantly for people in areas with government subsidies on solar power generation, the rate paid by the grid can rise as high as $0.80/kWh, so you’re all of a sudden looking at $2650.  Woah.

Choosing an MPPT Charge Controller – Amp Rating

This barely deserves its own section because it’s pretty straightforward, but charge controllers obviously come in a wide variety of sizes, which is measured by their amp rating.  My Morningstar Tristar 45 MPPT has the 45 to indicate 45 amps is the most it can handle.  430 watts panel output / 12 volt battery voltage = 36 amps and since the next smallest model is 30 amps, the choice of 45 was dead simple, hopefully you can easily do the same comparison yourself, perhaps leaving a bit of room if you feel like adding more panels in the future.

Choosing an MPPT Charge Controller – Competing Brands

Now that we’ve done all the mathematical heavy lifting, all that remains is to pick an actual controller.  Xantrex, Outback and Morningstar are the dominant brands on the market, so it’s just up to you to decide which customizability and extra features you need (temperature compensation, LCD display, customizable charging set points, PC monitoring software, accessories like relay controllers to turn on and off other system components, etc).  As I am so pleased with my Morningstar Tristar MPPT, I’ve written an additional post detailing all the features that make it such an enticing MPPT charge controller.

——————————————————————————————-

So that’s how to select the best charge controller.  Over the coming weeks I will be creating posts for each aspect of the creation of off-grid solar power systems with the hopes that you can follow along and use the the info for your own DIY solar panel system.  Of course it gets a little technically involved in spots, so feel free to ask for clarification in the comments or drop me an e-mail.

Solar Power System Sizing – How much power do you need?

Best Solar Panels – Selecting the best solar panels for you

Solar Batteries – Selecting the best solar batteries for you

item.title: Just Another Day at the Office in Quartzsite AZ
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: What bothers me is that I actually have a plan and I’m executing it. Two weeks ago I said I needed to go park in the middle of the desert away from any distractions and be productive, and here I am. Even at the time I wavered, contemplating robbing banks or selling drugs as I’ve [...]
item.content:encoded:
What bothers me is that I actually have a plan and I’m executing it.  Two weeks ago I said I needed to go park in the middle of the desert away from any distractions and be productive, and here I am.  Even at the time I wavered, contemplating robbing banks or selling drugs as I’ve always joked, but unfortunately no.  For five days I’ve been camped out on BLM lands 6 miles south of Quartzsite AZ…working.

My office in Quartzsite AZ

I haven’t moved more than 10 yards in that timeframe, I haven’t spoken to a soul, I certainly haven’t showered or shaved.  I eat and drink the food and water I packed in, I harvest the energy of the sun to power my laptop tethered to my phone to access the internet to hock various products on various websites in what are but the crude, malnourished saplings of “internet business”.  It’s a necessary evil, but being the first time I’ve done such “work” for personal commercial gain in oh, a year, it obviously makes me hearken back to the good ol’ days which I jokingly refer to with new acquaintances I meet on the road as “when I used to be a normal person”.  As you can well imagine, I take stock of what lines illicit the best response after telling my story about a hundred times, and that one ranks quite highly.

Problem is, the old necessary evil had no beginning or end, no means or justification.  This evil is mine and mine alone, so I can just put it on pause, drive to from Quartzsite AZ to Phoenix AZ and party.  But Phoenix scares me, all I can picture is old people, mega malls, firearms and Christianity.  It is but two hours away and I will likely drive there Thursday to watch my NASCAR and spring training baseball (as also foreshadowed), then turn around and return to the desert.

Tell me that rock doesn't look like an 18th century lady serving tea

Realizations, several of them occur rapid fire now that I have nothing but time to think, and I welcome it.  One, I need but $12000 a year to maintain this lifestyle.  Self-employed or not, think what amount of effort you would need to procure that amount of money yourself.  Hopefully the answer is minimal.  Two, $12000 a year is right on the so-called poverty line, yet in my mind I live like a king.  Three, I once had visions, aspirations that I could yell these things at people that they could do it too themselves and be free, to which I now fully understand they would respond “free to live in a van, alone in the middle of the desert?”  And they would be correct.  Perhaps I am uniquely adapted, or perhaps it is a grotesque mutation as they are often one in the same.

You know what, scratch that, you should probably quit your job and be free to live in a van in the middle of the desert.  At least I didn’t yell that.

item.title: Joshua Tree Camping
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: I wouldn’t call it Joshua Tree camping so much as Joshua Tree surviving. With so many miles of vast and pristine desert wilderness (as pictured in the gallery) you’d better be prepared for coyotes wandering through your campsite lured by the lamb shanks you’re cooking in the open fire, not to mention rattlesnakes, scorpions and [...]
item.content:encoded:
I wouldn’t call it Joshua Tree camping so much as Joshua Tree surviving.  With so many miles of vast and pristine desert wilderness (as pictured in the gallery) you’d better be prepared for coyotes wandering through your campsite lured by the lamb shanks you’re cooking in the open fire, not to mention rattlesnakes, scorpions and tarantulas, although I was lucky enough to only come across the first creature, and he was nothing but curious.  There is no water or electricity at any of the 10 official Joshua Tree camping grounds so you best pack that in yourself.  Cell phone reception or internet you can totally forget, which explains why I was incommunicado the last 5 days.

The views are unreal

I wouldn’t have even noticed the coyote while I was tending to the fire if it wasn’t for my Quebecois friend Raphael from Trois Riviere.  Having rolled in around 4 PM to Hidden Valley campground, the first one you hit from the main north entrance, I saw the sign read FULL, so did a quick survey, saw nothing and wound up staying the night at Ryan.  I wizened up the next day at noon when I drove back into Hidden Valley to scope the first open spot that it’s more just because the rangers only come by to flip the sign every few days.  There were plenty available so I grabbed an absolutely stunning spot nestled in with some boulders and a view across the expansive desert behind me.

Stunning Barker Dam

After doing the two nearby day hikes of the visually mind boggling Barker Dam and drastically less interesting Wall Street Mill, I was already afraid someone would steal my spot so to return and find a bunch of water and camping gear hidden in the rocks was somewhat disconcerting.  It turned out to be no problem at all though as it was just Raphael’s stuff and had been there all along.

He had a great trick of just pitching his tent in amongst the boulders and staying there for free having hitched into camp from Palm Springs after taking the bus there from Vancouver.  Joshua Tree happens to be one of the climbing meccas of North America with its huge array of varying sizes and difficulties of boulders to scramble up, and Raphael had been doing just that for a full month.  To hear he only spent $250 during that entire stretch definitely put me to shame, but he ate Ramen noodles and canned tuna while I feasted on lamb, corn, roasted red pepper and whiskey, so I’ll take my monetary licks any day.

The Wild West

Raphael had it figured out for sure.  Beyond his tips on the wisdom of not really having to pay because the rangers never came by and screw it because the place was free when he first came 8 years ago before the California budget crisis, he also well understood this fabled “work-life balance”.  Six months a year he cycles through Europe and climbs here or in Red Rocks, the other six months he does seasonal work like picking cherries in the Okanagan and king crab fishing in Alaska.  Naturally I am told it’s nothing at all like the TV show, they work at most 6 hours a day while living on the beach in July.

As for the park itself, I am torn whether it is actually better than the redwoods in terms of nature and is perhaps the first place of my entire trip I will tell people “you have to go here”.  If you’re anywhere near LA, it’s only 2 hours away and more than worth the trip.  Everything feels like a scene out of a Clint Eastwood spaghetti western, or to modernize it, Red Dead Redemption (this is the best video game of all time FYI, if you haven’t played it, get it).

Freaky deaky trees

Wait, I totally just ruined it even trying to compare the place to anything, because there’s really nothing like it.  The Joshua trees themselves just blend into the atmosphere after awhile because the place is so much more than that.  They were gifted their name by Mormon settlers who saw the branches extended to the heavens so naturally gave them a good old fashioned biblical name, but even I could feel the obvious spirituality of the place.  A fellow next to me on the peak of Ryan Mountain exclaimed he felt like he was at the center of the universe.  He also happened to be from Vancouver and a Canucks fan, so his quip about the Calgary Flames almost landed him an express ticket to said spiritual heavens via a more direct route down the side of the mountain with a helpful push from yours truly.

Uhhh…too much to say, check out the gallery, it’s definitely my best yet.

Addendum of interesting facts:

Wild rock formations

-100 years ago it rained twice as much here as it does now.  When I heard about pioneers raising cattle I scoffed at them as insane, but things change and it once actually made sense, although I can’t think of a more desolate, frightening place to live unless I had a ranch with about a dozen people on it.

-A process occurs in the soil here to reverse erosion caused by cryptobiotic bacteria that actually bond sand back together again into a crust.

-Most of the good stuff is in the high desert at the north end of the park, but if you want free Joshua Tree camping (other than the ol’ not paying trick) there’s free BLM lands you can park an RV or pitch a tent on directly outside the south entrance within sight of sign.  Backcountry tent camping is also allowed for free almost anywhere in the park as long as you’re 1 mile from the road and register your vehicle.

item.title: Hollister Brewing Company
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: I was immediately wary of the place because of the name, afraid the J. Crew Bar & Grill would be next door, but no, it just happens to be on Hollister Road in the town of Goleta, which is attached to Santa Barbara. It’s in a large big box shopping center which is my first [...]
item.content:encoded:
I was immediately wary of the place because of the name, afraid the J. Crew Bar & Grill would be next door, but no, it just happens to be on Hollister Road in the town of Goleta, which is attached to Santa Barbara.  It’s in a large big box shopping center which is my first time experiencing such a strange brewery location, but with the Kmart across the street allowing overnight RV parking, I thought I’d head over.

Pretty welcoming front entrance

I learned a new verb in San Francisco when I asked someone where to find good sushi and they replied “I dunno, just yelp it” and I’ve been checking the site from time to time ever since.  In the case of Hollister Brewing, the reviews were bang on, absolutely top notch beers with tons of variety and a brew master who knew what he was doing and wasn’t afraid to take chances, but with forgettable, overpriced food.

Wandering in around 4 PM, the stools by the bar were half full with several 50 year old male regulars, and that trend would continue throughout the night.  I get the feeling it’s the place people in the surrounding offices stop in after work before heading back to the wife and kids, so not exactly lively, but certainly good for trading war stories.  It’s bright and open with aluminum finish and a view into the brewery and kitchen and before 6 PM a pint of any beer they make under 8% alcohol is only $3.  At first I was slightly peeved to find they were only 16 oz. pints, but when you’re getting 7.6% IPA’s that pack a walloping punch of flavour to boot, the reduced size is probably good from a personal safety standpoint.  And there were at least 3 beers that day (it changes often I’m told) that were 10% or higher.

Wicked variety

Wanting to avoid going from zero to hero, I started with their India Brown Ale, a combination I had yet to come across and one that tasted just as you’d expect from the name.  It was basically a slightly hoppy Newcastle, a bit sweeter and thicker on the malt and with a back and roof of the mouth hops tingling, not a pronounced bite.  It was well executed enough I knew I’d be trying a few so asked for a taste of their Bushwick Stout on nitro.  It was creamy, very nutty, and surprisingly light but before I could go for a full pint, my barstool friend Marlon beside me offered up his wisdom that I should get it on cask and that he’d pick it up for me, wanting to leave the wandering Canadian with a positive impression of his favourite bar.

Not afraid to try different brews

Marlon was a hulking man, but one that you gathered after 15 seconds was gentle as a teddy bear, and he certainly knew his beer and the ins and outs of Hollister.  The cask version of the Bushwick was easily twice as good as the nitro, due to the lack of carbonation it became twice as thick, still wasn’t bitter in the slightest and by the end of the pint had built up an oatmeal richness on the tongue, even though it was made from barley.  As Marlon and I discussed some of Kafka’s writings as he had studied them in university 20 years prior, I was in no mood to correct him that the man was Czech, not German, and he was on his way out anyways.

He was soon replaced by a dreadlocked fellow who I learned did ceramics work at UCSB just down the street.  As I ordered a pint of their Hippie Kicker IPA, the guy told me usually all he deserved was a slap.  Two pints later he would storm out in disgust after getting into some sort of argument and pissing contest with an older yuppie gentleman about free climbing and who knew more people who had died up in Tahoe in the 80’s, I dunno, I mostly just sat and listened.

Super chill bartenders too

Oh right, the Hippie Kicker IPA.  I would rate this beast as the prototypical hoppy IPA, it had as much hops bing-POW high and low notes and lingering on the tongue as you’re going to find and basically destroyed my taste buds, but to stop in for one or two, it was a fantastic beer.  I wish I’d had it earlier before I tried their margherita pizza which had way over salted mozzarella, no tomatoes and too much crust, but was serviceable as drunken filler.

Like I said at the start, the beer is vastly superior to the food, perhaps even the best brews I’ve had all trip.

Taste: 4.6/5 (wide variety of delicious in-house brews, some with staggeringly high alcohol content)

Value: 4.25/5 ($3 pint happy hour, lots of interesting folk at the open bar stool area)

item.title: The SLO
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: That would be San Luis Obispo, pronounced slow. I never was able to figure out if it was SLO or the SLO. The first girl I asked was sitting alone at Bull’s Tavern which had attracted me with its $1.50 pints, which I’d soon discover were not full size, and the place was littered with [...]
item.content:encoded:
That would be San Luis Obispo, pronounced slow.  I never was able to figure out if it was SLO or the SLO.  The first girl I asked was sitting alone at Bull’s Tavern which had attracted me with its $1.50 pints, which I’d soon discover were not full size, and the place was littered with scum bags.  Anyways, this seemingly normal girl, sitting alone at the bar, I ask if she’s waiting for someone to join her or just chillin, she says “just chillin”.  So I continue, “OK then, I’m from Canada just passing through on a road trip, what’s your story?”

Go to the Frog & Peach for this back patio vibe

“Do you even want to know?” she shoots back, pointedly.

“Yeah, I’m just killin time, go for it.”  After an “OK, whatever” I learn in the course of 45 seconds that she was born and raised there, works for Diageo, and at some point when I tell her I actually know that’s the largest liquor distributor in the world and am super interested, she tells me she hates small talk and goes and sidles up with the grimiest motherfucker there.  Point taken, off to the Frog & Peach.

The bartender, she can tell just by the fact I’m there at 7 when it doesn’t start happening until 9 that I’m not from around, we chat while she slices lemons.  They have Murphy’s on tap which I didn’t even know existed outside of Ireland.  There’s no one inside so I head to the back patio because there’s a creek and some foot traffic to the nice restaurants.

The gum wall is quirky and cool, kinda like the town

I’m quickly joined at my picnic bench by three kids my age in the AmeriCorps.  I didn’t know that at the time, but coincidentally asked what AmeriCorps was in passing because I’d seen the word around.  Turns out to essentially be nature conservation work, be it maintaining trails or educating school groups and leading hikes and whatnot.  The catch is, you have to live on a military base, hence the “Corps”.  On a military base you aren’t allowed alcohol or to be intoxicated, even if you’re not in the military.

So these three kids had rented a hotel room for the night to come into town and get rip roaring drunk, and since they seemed to enjoy my merriment and not giving a fuck attitude, I was pulled along for the ride paying for only one of the dozen or so pitchers.  Not actually thinking about it until my stumbling, hiccupping walk back to the RV (no I lie, until the pounding headache the next morning), I haven’t actually been drunk since I left Canada.  I have beers all the time obviously, but not enough to lose my wits.

The old Mission is worth checking out

Perhaps I should lose my wits more often as I certainly had a passably normal conversation with at least 6 different groups of strangers after the AmeriCorps kids had started talking in made up British accents and falling into the flower bushes.  One random fellow told me that when I went to LA if I got lost in the wrong neighbourhood someone would pull me out the car door while upward stabbing through my rib cage into my heart so I would be dead in 10 seconds before I could see them tip my RV over, loot it, then light it on fire.  Perhaps a slightly graphic of a safety reminder that I was already well aware of, but I still don’t understand why they’d tip the RV over, it would be much easier to loot upright.

Another fellow I met was actually named Randy.  I told him he was my hero, that I pretended my name was Randy at restaurants, and probably said “RRRRRRrrrrrandy” about a dozen times.  Then after about a minute of chatting I asked “wait, what was your name again?” and when his response caused flashbacks to such a short period of time earlier, I knew it was probably time to go.

Oh, and I did put up a gallery, and it’s totally kosher to park an RV for a few days in front of the lawyer’s office at the end of Pacific Street past Santa Rosa.

item.title: City View Storage
item.dc:creator: Blimpy

item.content:encoded:
OK, parking isn’t exactly thrilling (although Treasure Island’s story contained in this post is), this is just a recommendation to fellow boondockers, or anyone driving through San Francisco looking for a place to put their motor vehicle.  Probably one of the best spots you’re going to find is City View Storage on Treasure Island.

The east view from Treasure Island

As I said, Treasure Island is a good story in and of itself.  Attached to Yerba Buena Island at the midpoint of the Bay Bridge connecting Oakland and San Francisco, Treasure Island is made up of leftover sea bottom dredge from building the Golden Gate Bridge and was constructed for the 1939 World’s Fair.  It’s flat as a board, no more than 10 feet above sea level at any point and having pretty nice views and being fairly large is a favourite destination of cyclists and joggers looking for an afternoon jaunt around movie production studios and low income housing.  It used to be a military base that has since been decommissioned, and now the bus runs 24/7 every 30 minutes right to the main terminal downtown making it easy to get to and from.

The west view from Treasure Island

Being San Fran, there are a few 21st century proposals out there to turn Treasure Island into a car-free, green, sustainable living community sometime in the near future, although with no way to or from other than the traffic-horrendous Bay Bridge (which has no pedestrian walkway), I’m not exactly sure how that’s supposed to work.  Coupled with the fact that the soil is so rich in radium and plutonium the EPA recommends against living there and the place will liquefy during an earthquake, it might be just another green daydream, but there are lots of palm trees!

Movie prop or radiation victim?

Back to City View Storage, I found the place online and was pleased to learn their RV rate is a mere $5 per foot per month.  As I was planning on crashing at a friend’s place and didn’t want to burden Bessie with hilly city driving, I could have left her there for a week and still been happy to only pay $115 to park an RV that close to San Fran.  In the end I left her there for 3 weeks in a razor wire fenced lot with a night watchman and had everything in perfect working order on my return.  Well, almost everything, let’s not count the emotional scarring involved in abandoning an RV you’ve lived in for 5 months straight.  I’m sorry girl, I’ll never do that again.

The lot is run by a young Scottish fellow my age who was more than accommodating, seemingly instantly replying to any e-mail or text I sent with questions or coordinating meeting up at the lot, and was even coincidentally there when I left to give a friendly goodbye.  And Bessie ran like a dream for the 100 miles I drove that day after three weeks of inactivity, which I attribute in no small part to Treasure Island’s radioactive soil.

item.content:encoded:
This is the fifth DIY solar post in a series on solar power systems, now onto the deep cycle battery for use as our solar batteries.  While this application was done for an RV solar panel system, the concepts are intended to apply for any do it yourself solar power system.  We hope you enjoy this entry (The Solar Series: Choosing Solar Batteries) and links to the rest of the DIY solar panel system series can be found at the bottom.

Choosing the type of solar batteries to fill the required capacity dictated by our solar power system sizing is one of the simpler steps as there are far fewer choices than with selecting panels.  The industry standard for solar batteries is the Trojan T-105 as they’re durable and cost effective, so you could skip this whole post and just pick up those.  However, if you’re trying to make the most informed decision or have specialized needs, let me go through some background on different battery technologies and manufacturers.

Battery Applications – Deep Cycle Battery VS Starter Battery

Although this series of posts is intended to apply beyond just RV solar panel systems, that does provide us a good base to compare different battery types.  Everyone knows a standard automobile has a starter battery under the hood.  Its main purpose is to provide a very high current in a short burst to turn over the starter motor to get the engine going.  Its ability to do so is rated in Cold Cranking Amps (CCA) which will be higher for an 18-wheeler than a Honda Civic.  While a starter battery can hold a moderate amount of overall charge, that’s not its purpose.

Dual Purpose equals BAD!

This is where deep cycle solar batteries come in.  They are specialized for storing energy in applications that dissipate charge much more slowly than a starter battery and their capacity is rated in amp hours.  In my RV solar power system, when I have all the electronics going it will drain the solar batteries at 20 amps, where the capacity per battery is 110 amp hours (I have four).  A large starter battery can provide up to 200 amps for a few seconds but maybe only has a 60 amp hour capacity.

One point I have to make is there are batteries called “dual purpose” on the market which claim to provide the functionality of deep cycle and starter batteries in one handy package.  Naturally all this means is it’s bad at doing both of them.  I originally had one in my RV which I removed and replaced with a starter and put the solar batteries in a separate compartment in the back.  Avoid dual purpose batteries at all costs.

Battery Types – Flooded, Gel Cell & AGM

Flooded lead acid batteries are by far the most prevalent type of starter or deep cycle battery.  They contain conductive lead plates suspended in a battery acid liquid solution of electrolytes.  Starter batteries have a greater number of thinner plates for maximum surface area and maximum current, whereas deep cycle batteries have a lesser number of thicker plates to store more charge.

Sorta the idea via Wikipedia

Flooded lead acid is the oldest battery technology so is the cheapest, and if treated correctly more than adequately durable.  Because the electrolyte solution is just water with dissolved battery acid ions, it can evaporate over time, or convert to hydrogen and oxygen gas if the batteries are overcharged, requiring an occasional top-up with distilled or de-ionized water.  One variation to offset this is sealed lead acid batteries where this gas cannot easily escape.

Gel Cell batteries function exactly the same as flooded, except the electrolyte is replaced with a gel.  This means the batteries don’t need to be held upright, are less sensitive to vibration and the electrolyte will not evaporate.  However, they are more expensive.

AGM stands for absorbed glass mat and is the newest and most expensive technology.  Here the electrolyte is held next to the plates by a fibreglass mesh.  They are more resistant to extreme temperatures, hold more charge per unit of weight and don’t have the electrolyte evaporate or need to be upright, partially justifying their cost.

Deep Cycle Battery Manufacturers

Trojan

Trojan – I already mentioned Trojan because they’re the brand I chose and are very popular for RV and off-grid solar power systems.  Their classic T-105 is a 6 volt flooded lead acid designed for golf carts, which just so happens to work perfectly for RV solar batteries as well.  Keep in mind you’ll need to buy them in pairs to achieve the required 12 volts.  They sell several other voltage and capacity combinations, so if there’s a distributor in your area, investigate after researching on their website.

Surette

Surette/Rolls – Another heavyweight in the renewable energy and transportation deep cycle and solar battery industry, Surette specializes in more heavy duty applications and is slightly harder to find.  However, their products are well reviewed, they have more variety especially in larger battery banks, so they’re definitely worth looking into (website here).

East Penn – Another well known battery manufacturer, they manufacturer more conventional consumer batteries, something like an AC/Delco.  Their EPGC15G is similar to the T-105, and they also have a variety of Gel and AGM batteries such as the 8A27 I was also recommended (website here).

East Penn

Other – I listed three big players, and like I said there isn’t a huge variety in batteries because they aren’t overly complicated so manufacturers succeed by making a lot of them well with small profit margins.  If you want to try another company, make sure you research their products and ensure you get good product data (explained next section).  While sourcing batteries locally can be cheaper due to their weight, when they are shipped drained there are some good deals online for the T-105s.  Lastly, I 100% recommend against used batteries.  I saw some great deals on Craigslist in my area, but you have no idea how they were (mis)treated before you got them and they could die sooner than you hoped, ruining the value proposition.

Solar Battery Parameters

As I mentioned, the above established manufacturers will be able to tell you a lot about each of the solar batteries they make, which you can use to make them last as long as possible, which is really the only concern once installed.

Voltage Set Points – When my solar batteries are 100% charged, have been allowed to rest for several hours and have no current being drawn from them, they settle around 12.6 Volts, which is fairly standard.  While you would hope you could just apply a voltage of 12.6 to them during the day to return them to full charge, unfortunately it doesn’t work this way…at all.  I don’t want to get into the nitty gritty, and will touch on it more in the Charge Controller post, but a voltage somewhat above this 12.6 is required during the bulk charge, then once it reaches full charge it needs to be held there for a specific period of time, then to prevent overcharging it needs to be lowered to a specific float voltage.  These all vary per battery and without knowing the exact numbers, you won’t be able to achieve peak charging efficiency or battery life.

Capacity Degredation VS Cycles – There isn’t really a formal term for this variable but you’ll usually find it as a graph.  All it indicates is that over time, a battery’s capacity will decrease each time it is discharged and recharged.  What counts as a ‘cycle’ can vary, usually 50% discharge is the number because below that isn’t good for the batteries.  As the three manufacturers listed above are all reliable and competitors, you’ll find they’ll be fairly good and in line with each other that sometime after 500 cycles there will be a rapid decline in how much a battery can hold.  This also illustrates the importance of not overdrawing your battery bank.

Selecting Batteries

I chose Trojan T-105s, but they're all this heavy

Now that I’ve outlined all the considerations around different solar battery manufacturers and types, and you’ve figured out which are available in your area, I wanted to finish with a quick and easy comparison method between two or more different batteries.  It’s just two simple numbers derived from a spreadsheet.  The first is dollars per amp hour ($/AH) and measures cost effectiveness, the second is amp hours per pound (AH/lb) and measures weight effectiveness, which is only important for mobile applications and even then not a huge factor unless comparing flooded to AGM.  Simply fill in the blanks yourself following this example.

Mfgr Surette East Penn Trojan
Model S-460 EPGC15G T-105
Cost ($) 310 189 186
Capacity (AH) 350 215 225
Weight (lb) 117 63 62
$/AH 0.89 0.88 0.83
AH/lb 2.99 3.41 3.63

As I said right off the bat, I picked the cheapest and most readily available Trojans and they’ve worked great ever since.

——————————————————————————————-

So that’s it on the selection of solar batteries.  Over the coming weeks I will be creating posts for each aspect of the creation of off-grid solar power systems with the hopes that you can follow along and use the the info for your own DIY solar panel system.  Of course it gets a little technically involved in spots, so feel free to ask for clarification in the comments or drop me an e-mail.

After doing the dirty deed (they had a donation box of all things next [...]
item.content:encoded:
Sparing you any of the gory details, I knew it was time to empty Bessie’s tanks at a Sani-Dump, so I searched online for the nearest free one, which turned out to be Harris Beach State Park just north of Brookings.  After doing the dirty deed (they had a donation box of all things next to it), I thought I’d take a wander before heading into town.  Seeing a sign for a Marine Garden, I took a look around and thought “well this just looks like a bunch of hedges” so decided to head down a rocky set of switchbacks to the beach below.

The arch has a calming effect

It was quite the amazing scene to have stumbled on through nothing more than excrement-related fluke.  There was a brilliant set of tidal pools filled with hermit crabs, anemones, star fish and all variety of plant life shielded by a large and narrow natural arch that calmed the incoming sea waves to allow the pools to exist.  To the right of the arch was a massive array of mussels and barnacles clung to the rocks in much more turbulent patches of tide.  On both sides out in the harbour there were sea lions and birds galore.

Anemone is hard to spell

The place was truly alive containing some of the most varied flora and fauna I have ever seen packed into what couldn’t have been more than 100 yards long.  I hopped from rock to rock snapping photos like a madman for at least 20 minutes until I finally realized “ohhh, this is the marine garden!”  The lady in the pink hoodie in one of the shots confirmed my suspicion and told me she and her husband had called in sick to work and done the same with their 4 kids in school for what she figured would be the last blast of beautiful weather for the year.  My kind of gal for sure, she had more spunk and curiosity than her 4 teenagers combined jumping around and poking her head in whatever pool she could find.  Mentioning that it was never above 70 degrees this time of year, I replied “oh that’s just because I’m here.”  She giggled at the silliness of the fedora-adorned Canadian, but the funny part is, I wasn’t joking.

I waited 5 minutes for this to happen again, it didn't

For me the highlight was looking at a patch of mussels curiously high up on some rocks and thinking “but how do they get any water or food up there?”  Sure enough the next wave came crashing in right over top of all of them, yielding what has to be one of my favourite shots, although there have been countless over the last 72 hours.  And that’s just the point, 24, 48, 72 in the titles, all of this happened in a three day stretch.  Oregonaturemagikal was meant to be more a description of the photojournal, but then I got to typing, so either way flip through some of the pictures (Umpqua, Gold Beach, Brookings), you won’t regret it.

Bessie likes

Oh, and just to top it all off then I went and parked overnight right on the banks of the Chetco River Jetty in Brookings with the ocean crashing away just a stone’s throw to my left.  I think the view is the first picture I’ve taken inside Bessie looking out the whole trip, and compared to the last 72 hours, yeah, I guess it’ll have to do.  Sigh, now I have to drive to California and the redwood forests, it’s a tough life.

item.content:encoded:
Deciding to abandon Bandon, I set off for the much sexier sounding Gold Beach.

Another boondocking gem

Seeing a couple of recommended roadside turnouts to camp at in my pimped out GPS, and having slept in one before no problem, I decided to go for it.  There were plenty along this winding, cliff-top stretch of Highway 101, mostly for viewpoints that I’m sure would have worked fine, but I figured these two spots were listed for a reason.  They were, as you can see from the attached shot taken the second I put the RV in park and jumped out.  Now with giant boulders draped in green, the scene had taken on a more rugged, Irish feeling, although I didn’t notice the green until the next day with it being sunset.

I should use my tripod more

Taking my usual waves and sunset shots, but this time with some nice big ol’ rocks for variety, I headed back to Bessie to call it a night…except it was 7 PM.  Once the darkness set in and I overcame the jitters I got when someone pulled into the turnout (likely to check their map, not to eat me) I noticed peering out my windows that I could see outside pretty darn well.  Perfectly clear skies and a big three quarter moon lit things up nicely enough that I wanted to bust out the tripod and try some night shots for the first time.

Just so you know it's dark out

Having never done this before, I decided to start big and jack the shutter speed waaay up to 13 seconds.  Woah!  Looking at the camera’s LCD screen startled me.  If I didn’t say anything, you’d think it was broad daylight, but no, the light’s all still there, our eyes just aren’t sensitive enough to see it in colours.  That freaked me out a lot, and it wasn’t until the next day I noticed another long shutter excursion somehow got me a shot of Mars, Venus or a satellite.  I don’t know which, but it sure wasn’t red like that when I was snapping pictures.

Return to light

I feel bad for all the people that pulled in at sunset or the following morning to take pictures for 2 minutes, as I spent a full 18 hours there.  The totality of the experience is something I absorbed to be a part of me, the pictures convey mere fragments of it.  Watching a full cycle of day to night and back, the stoic and jagged rocks only betrayed two hints of their transience, the rise and fall of the tide and how they reflected ambient light.  But wandering along the beach in bare feet, the sand here is very coarse, made of battered barnacle bits, and of course those very rocks.
